findings.claim: Narrowing `set`'s key parameter from `PropertyKey` to `string` is a source-breaking change for callers that use symbol or numeric keys.
findings.rationale: `PropertyKey` is `string | number | symbol`. Using unique symbols as context-variable keys is a common pattern for third-party middleware to avoid name collisions, and numeric keys are also legal. After this change `c.set(MY_SYMBOL, v)` / `c.set(1, v)` fail to compile even though the underlying `Map` still stores them fine at runtime. If the intent is only to tighten the `IsAny` fallback, the concrete parameter type probably should stay `PropertyKey` (or the change needs a semver-major note). Reasonably confident this is at least worth an explicit decision; it is a public API signature.

findings.claim: `Record<PropertyKey, any>` -> `Record<string, any>` in the `IsAny<E>` fallback may desynchronize `set` from the corresponding `get`/`var` types.
findings.rationale: This fallback exists so that when `E` is `any` every key is accepted. Restricting it to `Record<string, any>` means symbol/number keys are rejected in the untyped-env case too. If the sibling `get` overload (and the `var` getter) still use `PropertyKey`/`Record<PropertyKey, any>`, the two sides now disagree: a value could be readable by a key shape that is no longer writable. Worth checking that `get`, `var`, and the internal `#var` map declaration were updated consistently in the same change; if only `set` was touched, this is an inconsistency bug.

findings.claim: Runtime still accepts non-string keys while the type says `string`, so the narrowing is unenforced at runtime.
findings.rationale: `this.#var.set(key, value)` stores whatever is passed, so JS callers (or `as any` casts) can still insert symbol/number keys, and `get` will still return them. This makes the type narrowing purely cosmetic and can hide the breakage from tests that go through untyped paths — low confidence that action is needed, but it means the change buys no actual safety.
